content: The slower rate and extended time required for cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) fungal clearance when using fluconazole compared to amphotericin B has led to specific treatment recommendations. These guidelines apply to all age groups, including individuals with HIV who have previously received antiretroviral therapy (ART) but develop cryptococcal meningitis due to ART failure, those transitioning to second-line ART, and those restarting ART after an interruption. Although there is limited direct evidence, the consensus among experts is that ART modifications should be delayed by four weeks after an amphotericin B-based induction regimen or 4–6 weeks after a fluconazole-based induction regimen in ART-experienced individuals. There is no prospective evidence to guide the timing of ART initiation in asymptomatic individuals with cryptococcal antigenemia who are receiving preemptive antifungal therapy. However, the Southern African HIV Clinicians’ Society recommends starting ART two weeks after initiating fluconazole. Immediate ART initiation may be considered if lumbar puncture excludes cryptococcal meningitis in individuals testing positive for whole-blood cryptococcal antigen. ART-experienced individuals with cryptococcal meningitis should be evaluated for potential underlying ART failure, ideally confirmed with an HIV viral load test. ART switches should be deferred for four weeks following an amphotericin B-based induction regimen or 4–6 weeks after a fluconazole-based induction regimen. Discontinuation of fluconazole maintenance therapy (secondary prophylaxis) is recommended for adults, adolescents, and children over five years of age living with HIV who have successfully treated cryptococcal disease (meningeal or non-meningeal). This is advised if the individual has been stable on ART and antifungal maintenance therapy for at least one year, with a CD4 count ≥100 cells/mm³ and a fully suppressed viral load. In settings without viral load monitoring, discontinuation is recommended if the CD4 count is ≥200 cells/mm³. For children aged 2–5 years, discontinuation is advised if they have been stable on ART and antifungal therapy for at least one year, with a CD4 percentage >25% or an absolute count >750 cells/mm³. Maintenance therapy should not be discontinued in children under two years of age. Secondary prophylaxis should be restarted if the CD4 count drops below 100 cells/mm³ in adults, adolescents, and children over five years, or below 25% or 750 cells/mm³ in children aged 2–5 years, or if a WHO stage 4 clinical event occurs, regardless of age. While CD4 monitoring is no longer routinely recommended for ART response in settings with viral load testing, it remains critical for guiding decisions on discontinuing fluconazole maintenance therapy. Few studies have assessed the risk of recurrent disease after discontinuing maintenance therapy. A systematic review found a very low recurrence rate among individuals who discontinued therapy with a CD4 count >100 cells/mm³ after completing induction and consolidation antifungal therapy and achieving sustained immune recovery on ART. The higher CD4 threshold for discontinuation (≥200 cells/mm³) accounts for the widespread use of less effective oral fluconazole monotherapy, limited viral load access, and infrequent CD4 monitoring in lowand middle-income countries. Discontinuation at a lower threshold (CD4 >100 cells/mm³) is advised if viral load monitoring confirms suppression on ART. Optimal timing for discontinuing maintenance therapy in individuals with localized non-meningeal disease (e.g., pulmonary disease) or isolated serum cryptococcal antigen positivity remains undetermined. Limited data exist on adolescents and children, but the same principles of sustained ART-related immune reconstitution should apply. A feasibility assessment conducted in 16 countries across Africa, Asia, and Latin America identified significant barriers to diagnosing and treating cryptococcal disease. These include limited access to rapid diagnostics, suboptimal antifungal treatments, challenges in managing amphotericin B toxicity, and inadequate healthcare provider training. India ink remains the primary diagnostic test in many countries, with turnaround times ranging from hours to days. Rapid cryptococcal antigen tests are often unavailable or prohibitively expensive. Drug shortages, high costs, and poor forecasting further limit access to essential medications like amphotericin B and flucytosine, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa. In Asia, generic amphotericin B and fluconazole are more accessible, and national governments often provide these drugs free of charge. Amphotericin B toxicity monitoring practices vary widely, and preemptive hydration and electrolyte replacement are rare. Financial barriers and the burden on families often limit referrals to centers with monitoring capabilities. Efforts to improve outcomes should prioritize reliable access to rapid diagnostic tests, such as lateral flow assays, and essential antifungal medications. Advocacy is needed to reduce the cost of flucytosine and simplify drug registration procedures. National policies should provide clear guidance, supported by supervision systems and decision-making aids. The guidelines for diagnosing, preventing, and managing cryptococcal disease in HIV-infected individuals will be disseminated as a web-based product and incorporated into the next update of the WHO consolidated antiretroviral therapy guidelines. Dissemination efforts will include presentations at international conferences, workshops for country adaptation, and development of tools to assist resource-limited settings in implementing the recommendations.
